subject: religious-studies
title: Augustine on Human Nature
welcome_lead: Sit with the Bishop of Hippo as he meditates on the disordered will, the goodness of creation, and the necessity of grace.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR Religious Studies adventure on Augustine's anthropology: the Fall, original sin, concupiscence, and the necessity of grace.
final_note: You have grasped Augustine's account of human nature: created good, fallen in Adam, healed only by Christ's grace.

concepts.def: The pre-Fall state in which reason rightly governed will and passions.
Adam's primal disobedience, transmitted to all his descendants.
The disordered desire that remains as a wound even after baptism.
The 'lump of damnation' from which God elects some to salvation.
Disordered love that turns from God to creatures as ends in themselves.
Rightly ordered love which refers all created goods to God.

walkthroughs.h2: The Garden and the Pear Tree
walkthroughs.body_html: In Confessions II.4, Augustine narrates stealing pears as a boy 'not because I was hungry... but simply because it was not allowed'. The story illustrates his account of sin as perverse love: turning from God to a creature for its own sake. His Confessions, written around 397-400 AD, is a sustained meditation on grace ('thou hast made us for thyself, and our heart is restless until it rests in thee').

Augustine reads Genesis 3 (with Romans 5:12) as the historical occasion of a corruption transmitted to all humanity. After the Fall, the will retains freedom of choice but is in bondage to sin (non posse non peccare). Concupiscence, especially as disordered sexuality, transmits original sin biologically. Only baptism removes its guilt; concupiscence as wound remains.

Pelagius rejected Augustine's pessimism; the Synod of Carthage (418) sided with Augustine. The Council of Orange (529) confirmed prevenient grace. Modern critics like Reinhold Niebuhr accept the diagnosis but reinterpret it existentially. Feminist theologians criticise Augustine's reading of Eve and his treatment of sexuality as the vehicle of sin.
